title: “SHOULD HE TREAT OUR SISTER LIKE A PROSTITUTE?” — THE QUESTION THAT EXPOSED A FAMILY, A VIOLENT WORLD, AND OUR DESPERATE NEED FOR JESUS
paragraphs: “SHOULD HE TREAT OUR SISTER LIKE A PROSTITUTE?” — THE QUESTION THAT EXPOSED A FAMILY, A VIOLENT WORLD, AND OUR DESPERATE NEED FOR JESUS

She was violated. Her father remained silent at first. Her brothers answered with bloodshed. And somewhere between the scandal and the slaughter, a wounded woman's voice disappeared. What happens when the pursuit of justice becomes another expression of sin?
Some wounds never make a sound.
Some people carry memories they cannot speak about, cry over things nobody knows, and spend years trying to recover something another person took from them without permission.
And sometimes, the deepest wound is not only what someone did to you.
It is what the people who were supposed to protect you did afterward.
Genesis 34 contains one of the most disturbing stories in the Old Testament. There are no comforting miracles, no easy resolutions, and no beautiful ending neatly wrapped around the suffering.
There is a young woman named Dinah.
There is a man who violates her.
There is a father whose initial silence is recorded.
There are brothers whose anger turns into a massacre.
And there is a question that closes the chapter like a blade piercing the human conscience:
“Should he deal with our sister as with an harlot?” — Genesis 34:31 (KJV)
In the original Hebrew, the question reads:
הַכְזוֹנָה יַעֲשֶׂה אֶת־אֲחוֹתֵנוּ
Ha-khezônāh ya‘ăśeh ’et-’ăḥôtēnû?
A close translation is:
“Should he treat our sister like a prostitute?”
The Hebrew word zônāh (זוֹנָה) refers to a prostitute. But notice something profoundly important.
Jacob's sons were not declaring that Dinah was a prostitute. They were protesting the degrading way she had been treated.
Their question expressed outrage over the violation of their sister's dignity.
And yet, the tragedy of this story is that men who recognized one terrible injustice went on to commit another.
That is what makes Genesis 34 so painfully relevant today.
Because human beings can be right about what they condemn and terribly wrong about how they respond.
You can recognize evil while allowing evil to grow inside your own heart.
You can defend someone you love while becoming someone they never needed you to become.
You can begin with righteous anger and end with unrighteous vengeance.
Dinah was the daughter of Jacob and Leah. Genesis 34:1 tells us that she went out to see the women of the land.
Then Shechem, the son of Hamor, saw her.
Genesis 34:2 records what happened using three significant Hebrew verbs:
Lāqaḥ (לָקַח) — to take.
Shākab (שָׁכַב) — to lie with.
‘Innâ (עִנָּה) — to afflict, humiliate, or violate.
Together, within this narrative, these words describe a sexual violation.
Scripture does not present Dinah as responsible for what Shechem did. Her decision to go out does not excuse his actions.
Being present somewhere is not consent.
Being noticed is not consent.
Being vulnerable is not permission.
The shame of sexual violence belongs to the person who commits it, not the person who suffers it.
What makes the passage even more disturbing is what happens next.
Genesis 34:3 says that Shechem became deeply attached to Dinah, loved her, and spoke tenderly to her.
But tenderness afterward does not erase violence beforehand.
Affection does not retroactively create consent.
A desire for marriage does not undo a violation.
Someone can speak beautifully while having acted wickedly.
Someone can claim to love you while refusing to respect your dignity.
Perhaps somebody reading this understands that more deeply than they ever wanted to.
You remember the apologies. The promises. The affectionate words that followed the pain. The moments when you wondered whether what happened was really as terrible as you remembered.
Hear this carefully.
You do not have to reinterpret someone else's wrongdoing simply because they later expressed affection.
Biblical love does not rejoice in wrongdoing but rejoices with the truth (1 Corinthians 13:6).
God does not require you to call evil good in order to prove that you are a forgiving Christian.
Then Jacob heard what had happened to his daughter.
Genesis 34:5 says that he held his peace until his sons returned from the fields.
Scripture does not fully explain his motives. We should not pretend to know everything happening inside his heart.
But the silence is there.
And for anyone who has ever disclosed a painful experience only to be met with hesitation, indifference, or concern about the family's reputation, that silence may feel painfully familiar.
Sometimes people are more concerned about avoiding scandal than confronting sin.
They worry about what the neighbors will say.
What the church will think.
What will happen to the family name.
What protecting the wounded might cost them.
But a reputation preserved through the concealment of wrongdoing is not righteousness.
Jesus never taught us to protect appearances at the expense of truth.
Ephesians 5:11 tells believers not to participate in the unfruitful works of darkness but rather to expose them.
The Gospel is not an invitation to hide what is broken.
It is an invitation to bring what is broken into the light.
When Jacob's sons returned, Genesis 34:7 describes them as deeply grieved and very angry because Shechem had committed an outrage against Israel.
The Hebrew word used is nebālāh (נְבָלָה), a term describing disgraceful, morally outrageous conduct.
Their anger was not without reason.
Their sister had been violated.
Something had happened that should never have happened.
But anger, even when it begins with a legitimate cause, is not automatically holy in everything it produces.
That distinction may be one of the hardest lessons in the Christian life.
Hamor and Shechem approached Jacob's family seeking marriage arrangements. They offered economic opportunities, intermarriage, and the prospect of living together.
But Jacob's sons answered deceitfully.
They demanded that the males of the city be circumcised before any marriage arrangement could proceed.
Circumcision was not merely a cultural custom for Abraham's descendants. According to Genesis 17:10–11, it was the sign of God's covenant with Abraham.
Yet here, something sacred was manipulated for a destructive purpose.
They used the outward sign of a holy covenant as an instrument of deception.
And that should make every religious person uncomfortable.
Because it is possible to use the language of God while pursuing desires that do not reflect the character of God.
It is possible to quote Scripture while nurturing hatred.
To speak about holiness while practicing cruelty.
To invoke justice while secretly craving revenge.
To defend Christianity publicly while refusing to surrender our own sin privately.
Not everything done under the banner of religion has the approval of heaven.

Simeon and Levi eventually killed the males of the city, including Hamor and Shechem. They brought Dinah out of Shechem's house, and Jacob's other sons participated in plundering the city, taking possessions, women, and children.
Consider the terrible irony.
A woman had been violated.
And the response created more suffering for other women and children.
The brothers' outrage over their sister's degradation did not prevent them from inflicting suffering upon other families.
The wounded had become wounders.
And perhaps that is where this ancient story stops being merely ancient.
How many families have been destroyed because someone refused to stop passing their pain to another generation?
How many marriages have collapsed because betrayal became permission for another betrayal?
How many children have inherited anger that began long before they were born?
How many believers have mistaken their bitterness for discernment, their cruelty for courage, and their desire to punish others for spiritual conviction?
Pain can explain why we struggle.
It cannot make every response righteous.
James 1:20 declares:
“For the wrath of man worketh not the righteousness of God.”
The original Greek reads:
Orgē gar andros dikaiosynēn theou ouk ergazetai.
Human anger does not produce the righteousness of God.
That does not mean Christians must never experience anger. Ephesians 4:26 acknowledges anger while warning believers not to sin through it.
There is a difference between being angry because evil has occurred and allowing that anger to become the master of your soul.
There is a difference between pursuing accountability and wanting someone to suffer simply because you suffered.
There is a difference between justice and revenge.
Jacob confronted Simeon and Levi after the massacre, expressing concern about the danger their actions had brought upon his household.
And then came their unforgettable response:
“Should he treat our sister like a prostitute?”
It is the final question of Genesis 34.
The chapter ends without recording Dinah's own words.
We hear Shechem.
We hear Hamor.
We hear Jacob.
We hear the brothers.
But the woman at the center of the tragedy is given no recorded dialogue.
We must not invent her thoughts or claim to know what she felt. Scripture does not tell us.
Nevertheless, her absence from the recorded conversation invites us to consider something important about our own responses to suffering.
Are we actually listening to wounded people?
Or are we turning their suffering into an opportunity to express our own anger, defend our institutions, or prove our righteousness?
Sometimes the person everyone claims to be fighting for becomes the person nobody truly listens to.
If you have ever felt unheard in the middle of your own suffering, know that your value does not depend on how loudly others defend you.
Psalm 34:18 says:
“The LORD is nigh unto them that are of a broken heart.”
Your suffering is not invisible to God.
Your dignity is not determined by what someone did to you.
And your identity is not permanently defined by the worst chapter of your life.
You do not owe the internet your testimony or the details of your trauma. Those few words can be a prayer, an expression of faith, and a reminder to another hurting soul that they are not alone.
But Genesis 34 does not give Simeon and Levi the final moral verdict.
Years later, when Jacob spoke concerning his sons in Genesis 49:5–7, he condemned their violence and fierce anger.
“Cursed be their anger, for it was fierce; and their wrath, for it was cruel.”
Notice that Jacob cursed their anger, not their existence as human beings.
Their concern for Dinah did not make their massacre righteous.
Their sister's suffering did not grant them unlimited moral permission.
And yet, remarkably, the biblical story of Levi's descendants did not end with the violence of Genesis 34.
The tribe of Levi would later be set apart for sacred service, as recorded in Numbers 3:5–13 and Deuteronomy 10:8.
This does not mean the massacre was necessary, justified, or rewarded. Nor does Scripture explicitly describe the personal repentance of Simeon and Levi over this event.
But it does demonstrate that the history of a family can contain terrible sin without that sin becoming the entirety of its future.
God's redemptive purposes are not defeated by human failure.
And that brings us to Jesus Christ.
Because the ultimate answer to the darkness exposed in Genesis 34 is not found in another act of vengeance.
It is found at the cross.
Jesus entered a world filled with violence, exploitation, religious hypocrisy, injustice, and human pride.
He never treated vulnerable people as disposable.
He never confused mercy with moral compromise.
He never needed to deny the seriousness of sin in order to offer grace to sinners.
When Jesus suffered unjustly, 1 Peter 2:23 tells us that He did not retaliate but entrusted Himself to the One who judges righteously.
At Calvary, Jesus bore our sins.
Not because sin was insignificant.
Not because evil deserved to be ignored.
But because our redemption required something we could never accomplish through our own righteousness.
Romans 3:26 reveals God as both just and the justifier of those who have faith in Jesus.
At the cross, justice and mercy are not enemies.
God does not pretend that sin never happened.
Christ bears its terrible cost.
And through His death and resurrection, forgiveness and new life are offered to those who repent and believe.
This is why the Gospel is so much more powerful than revenge.
Revenge wants another person to experience your pain.
The Gospel confronts sin while offering transformation through Jesus Christ.
Revenge can destroy an enemy.
Christ can redeem a repentant sinner.
But let us never misunderstand forgiveness.
Forgiveness does not require a victim to return to an unsafe relationship.
It does not prohibit reporting a crime.
It does not eliminate appropriate legal consequences.
It does not demand immediate reconciliation or restored trust.
Romans 12:19 forbids personal vengeance, while Romans 13:1–4 recognizes the role of governing authorities in restraining wrongdoing.
A Christian can forgive while maintaining boundaries.
A Christian can pursue justice without cultivating hatred.
A Christian can seek professional help, protection, and accountability while trusting God.
And a person who has committed serious wrongdoing cannot use grace as an excuse to escape responsibility.
True repentance produces fruit consistent with repentance (Luke 3:8).
Grace is not permission to continue destroying people.
Grace calls us out of darkness and into a transformed life.
Perhaps you identify with the suffering surrounding Dinah's story.
Perhaps you know what it means to be disappointed by people who should have protected you.
Perhaps you recognize something of Simeon and Levi in yourself — an anger that began with a real wound but has slowly become something destructive.
Perhaps you have caused pain and spent years defending yourself instead of repenting.
Whatever brought you here, Jesus Christ calls you toward truth.
The wounded can seek refuge in Him.
The bitter can surrender their vengeance to Him.
The guilty can repent before Him.
The ashamed can discover that His mercy is greater than the condemnation of their past.
There is no promise that every earthly consequence will disappear.
But there is a promise that those who are in Christ are not condemned (Romans 8:1).
That is redemption.
That is the Gospel.
Jesus does not rewrite history by pretending the wounds never happened.
He redeems lives so that sin, suffering, shame, and failure do not have the final authority over those who belong to Him.
There may come a day when anger feels justified, forgiveness feels impossible, or someone else's wrongdoing threatens to consume your peace.
Come back to these truths.
Someone may be struggling with bitterness.
Someone may have misunderstood grace as permission to remain silent about abuse.
Someone may need to encounter Jesus again.
Ministry requires resources to continue, grow, create meaningful biblical content, and reach more people with the message of Jesus Christ.
Scripture recognizes the importance of supporting those who labor in teaching the Word (Galatians 6:6; 1 Corinthians 9:14).
As 2 Corinthians 9:7 reminds us, giving should come from the heart, not reluctantly or under compulsion, because God loves a cheerful giver.
Genesis 34 began with a woman whose dignity was violated.
It ended with a question about how she had been treated.

But the larger story of Scripture leads us toward a Savior who confronts evil, offers forgiveness to the repentant, draws near to the brokenhearted, and promises a future in which righteousness dwells.
One day, according to Revelation 21:4, God will wipe away every tear from the eyes of His people.
Until that day, we must protect the vulnerable, speak the truth, pursue justice, reject vengeance, repent of our own sins, and cling to Jesus.
Because what happened to you matters.
What you do with your pain matters.
And what Christ can accomplish through His redeeming grace matters more than the darkness that wants to define your future.
Do not let the evil that wounded you become the evil that lives through you. Bring your wounds to Jesus, and let His grace end what sin tried to continue.
